steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Qualitative data is non-numerical — it describes qualities or categories (e.g. eye colour, favourite subject).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Quantitative data is numerical — it can be measured or counted (e.g. height, number of pets).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Quantitative data splits into discrete and continuous.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Discrete data can only take specific values, usually whole numbers (e.g. number of siblings, shoe size).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Is 'number of goals scored in a match' discrete or continuous? | Q: Give an example of ordinal data. | Q: What is bivariate data?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Discrete — it can only take whole-number values (0, 1, 2, …). | Satisfaction rating (very dissatisfied, dissatisfied, neutral, satisfied, very satisfied). | Data that consists of pairs of values for two variables measured on the same individual, used to investigate relationships.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: If a value is counted, it is usually discrete; if it is measured, it is usually continuous. Shoe size is discrete even though half-sizes exist — it can only take set values. Temperature is continuous even though it is recorded to a set number of decimal places. When asked to classify data, give your answer and a brief justification. Bivariate data questions often link to scatter graphs and correlation.
